frameworks.name: Sales-to-Fulfillment Continuum
frameworks.definition: A spectrum where ease of selling and difficulty of fulfillment are inversely correlated: done-for-you is easy to sell and hard to fulfill; do-it-yourself is hard to sell and easy to fulfill.

frameworks.name: Done-For-You to Do-It-Yourself Pyramid (Tesla Model)
frameworks.definition: A top-down product sequencing strategy: start at the premium done-for-you tier (highest price, hardest to fulfill), build SOPs, then release done-with-you at one-third to one-fifth the price, then do-it-yourself at the lowest price; each layer productizes the layer above.

frameworks.name: One-on-One to Group Delivery Scaling Sequence
frameworks.definition: A progressive output-multiplication pattern for service delivery: one-on-one -> one-on-six -> one-on-twenty -> one-on-thirty -> train others to deliver; each step multiplies throughput while preserving most of the personalization value.

frameworks.name: Two Magic Customer Questions
frameworks.definition: Two inverted feature-priority questions: (1) If forced to keep only one feature, which would it be? (2) If forced to eliminate one feature with no consequence, which would it be? Together they produce a power ranking of value and waste.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that when a business owner says a tactic is unscalable, they almost always have a skill deficiency rather than a physics constraint. The tactic is not unscalable; the owner is insufficiently skilled to scale it. Examples like handwritten cards or one-on-one phone calls appear unscalable only because the owner lacks the hiring, training, or leverage knowledge to delegate them.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service businesses
High-touch tactics such as handwritten notes, onboarding calls, personal outreach
claims.mechanism: Every high-touch tactic has a 2.0 or 3.0 version achievable once the owner has capital and training knowledge; the tactic remains the same but delegation replaces founder labor.
bounded_by: Does not apply to tactics that are mathematically impossible to parallelize (e.g., founder-specific trust relationships that cannot be transferred)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that early-stage businesses making $0 in revenue cannot simultaneously be busy and broke. If an owner is truly busy doing the right revenue-generating activities, they will be earning; if they are broke, they have unused time they should fill with high-touch, seemingly unscalable customer-acquisition and onboarding tasks.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: you can't be busy and broke
conditions: Founders at $0 to low revenue who have available time
Service, community, or coaching businesses
claims.mechanism: Doing high-touch unscalable work generates both revenue and product/market learning simultaneously; idleness produces neither.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that in the early stages of a business, founders learn more per customer interaction than they earn. Engaging directly with customers at any price point (including $20/month) yields critical data on pain points, messaging hooks, product priorities, and conversion levers that cannot be obtained from analytics or assumptions alone.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: you learn more than you earn
conditions: Early-stage founders with fewer than a few hundred customers
Any service, community, or recurring-revenue business
claims.mechanism: Direct customer contact surfaces pain language, feature priority rankings, and conversion objections that the founder can immediately fold back into marketing copy and product design, compounding revenue per customer acquired.
bounded_by: At scale (hundreds of conversations per day), the marginal learning per call drops; the founder should shift from doing calls to systematizing insights.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that the done-for-you tier should be launched first, even though it is the hardest to fulfill, because the low customer count at launch means the operational burden is manageable, and each done-for-you engagement forces the development of SOPs that productize into lower-tier offerings later.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: start at the top of the pyramid
conditions: Service or agency businesses launching a new product line
Founder with low or no existing customer base
claims.mechanism: Small customer volume makes high-touch fulfillment operationally viable; SOPs generated from done-for-you work become the productized modules that power done-with-you and do-it-yourself tiers downstream.

numbers.axis: Relative price and fulfillment burden across tiers

bounded_by: Does not apply to technology products where marginal fulfillment cost is near zero regardless of tier order

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that every business incurs one of two types of debt during its early stages: financial debt (VC-backed companies paying market salaries upfront) or management debt (bootstrapped companies understaffed and operated by the founder doing multiple jobs). The founder must consciously choose which debt to carry through the early swamp period; the debt cannot be avoided.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Early-stage companies prior to positive cash flow
Applies to both venture-backed and bootstrapped business models
claims.mechanism: Without capital to hire at market rates, a founder fills multiple roles personally; this is analogous to taking on debt because the output of those roles must eventually be paid for (in hired salaries) to stop working overtime.
bounded_by: A business with strong early cash flow from a premium offer may be able to hire faster and avoid extended management debt

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that small businesses (under $10M revenue) have a structural competitive advantage over large businesses precisely because they can do high-touch, personalized, unscalable tactics that large businesses have systematized away. This advantage disappears as the business grows; therefore it must be maximized while available.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: the advantage of the small business
conditions: Businesses under $10M annual revenue
Competing against established or scaled players in the same category
claims.mechanism: Large companies have eliminated personalization to achieve scale efficiency; small companies can still personalize at no unit-economics cost, giving them a higher perceived value per customer touchpoint.

numbers.axis: Business size threshold for the small-business personalization advantage

bounded_by: Once the business reaches mid-market scale, the advantage shifts from personalization to reputation and resources

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that applying the two magic customer questions repeatedly across a large sample of customers produces a reliable power ranking of feature value. The first question (which feature is irreplaceable?) surfaces the highest-value element; the inverted second question (which feature would you remove with no consequence?) surfaces the least valuable element. Running both regularly allows systematic trimming toward the most universally valuable product configuration.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Businesses with at least a small existing customer base to query
Products with multiple features or service components
claims.mechanism: Customer answers aggregate into a frequency distribution; asking 100 customers yields a clear majority answer that reveals the product's real core value driver, allowing the founder to concentrate delivery and marketing on that element.

numbers.axis: Sample size needed for reliable power ranking

anchors.reliability: clear majority answer emerges (as stated by Hormozi)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the sales-to-fulfillment continuum shows that ease of selling and difficulty of fulfillment are inversely related for service businesses. Done-for-you is the easiest promise to sell and the hardest to deliver consistently; do-it-yourself is the hardest to sell and the easiest to deliver. Most early founders mistakenly start at the do-it-yourself end (hardest to sell), which is backwards.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service businesses (not technology/software products)
New product line launches or businesses starting from zero
claims.mechanism: Buyer motivation is highest when the seller takes maximal responsibility; shifting responsibility to the buyer via self-serve lowers the buyer's confidence in their own ability to achieve the outcome, reducing conversion.
bounded_by: Technology products are the primary exception: marginal cost of delivery is near zero regardless of tier, so the inverse relationship does not hold

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that transitioning from one-on-one delivery to group formats (one-on-six, one-on-twenty, one-on-thirty) can preserve close to the same perceived customer experience while multiplying throughput by five to six times per step. A business can reach 180 customers per day with a single person by scaling through group delivery milestones before training a second person.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: one on six, one on twenty, one on thirty
conditions: Service businesses where delivery is knowledge, coaching, onboarding, or structured presentation
The core message can be standardized into a repeatable presentation deck
claims.mechanism: Group delivery amortizes preparation time across more recipients; a standardized presentation preserves consistency while increasing audience size; multiplying the group size multiplies output without adding headcount.

numbers.axis: Daily customer throughput per delivery person across group-size milestones

bounded_by: Does not apply when the customer outcome is highly individualized and cannot be addressed by a standardized presentation

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that starting with the unscalable maximum-effort version of a tactic first, then extracting the highest-impact 20% of its components, allows a founder to build a scalable version that retains 80% of the effect at 10x the output. Committing cash from the low-scale version funds the build of the more leveraged version.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Businesses with any high-touch tactic that generates strong customer response
Founders who have completed enough repetitions to identify which elements drive the result
claims.mechanism: Doing the unscalable version repeatedly reveals via direct observation which components drive 80% of the outcome; cash from early sales funds delegation infrastructure; the scalable version replicates those high-impact components while cutting low-impact effort.

numbers.axis: Effect retention vs. output multiplier trade-off when scaling unscalable tactics

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a business owner looking 10 steps ahead and projecting the scalable future state back onto their current zero-revenue context is making the same error as someone who wants to get rich and therefore starts flying private immediately. The tactics appropriate to a wealthy outcome are outputs of wealth, not the path to it; adopting them prematurely destroys economics.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: Warren Buffett wasn't flying private to get rich
conditions: Early-stage founders at sub-$1M revenue who have zero or thin margins
Decisions about sales approach, team structure, or operational complexity
claims.mechanism: Wealthy operators give advice from their current resource context, not their early-stage context; applying that advice without matching resources increases cost without matching revenue, destroying unit economics.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that from a brand positioning perspective, launching done-for-you at the highest price first creates a price anchor for all subsequent tiers. Having 10 private clients paying $10,000/month makes it credible and appealing to offer a done-with-you program at a fraction of that price, because the anchor is established before the lower tier is introduced.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: you've price anchored the most expensive version
conditions: Service or coaching businesses introducing multiple tiers
Founder has at least a small number of premium clients generating results
claims.mechanism: The premium done-for-you tier builds an association between the founder and the highest-quality outcome; the done-with-you tier is positioned as access to that same system at reduced cost, making it feel like a bargain relative to the established anchor.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that the reason many high-touch tactics feel unscalable is that the founder lacks money, leverage, and context at the time they are evaluating the tactic, not because the tactic is physically impossible to scale. With unlimited capital and talent, any high-touch personalization can be scaled through hiring and training.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: you don't have the context from which to scale it
conditions: Founders evaluating whether to adopt a tactic before they can afford to delegate it
claims.mechanism: Perceived unscalability is a function of available resources, not physics; founders mistake their current resource constraint for a permanent ceiling on what is possible.
bounded_by: Physically impossible tasks (e.g., tasks that require the founder's personal identity or trust relationship) cannot be scaled regardless of resources

examples.text: Andy Frisella, founder of First Form (a supplement company doing hundreds of millions of dollars per year in revenue), started by writing handwritten cards to every single customer who bought a product. Initially Frisella wrote the cards himself. Over time he transitioned to only signing cards others had written. Eventually, other team members wrote and signed the cards entirely. The gesture and its customer-retention effect survived each transition, illustrating that a seemingly unscalable high-touch tactic can be delegated in stages while preserving most of its value.

A woman in the fitness world approached Alex Hormozi at an event and said her business was doing $30,000/month through outbound sales but she wanted a more scalable acquisition system. Hormozi challenged her assumption that outbound required people and was therefore unscalable, pointing out that fitness coaching delivery also requires people and is nonetheless scalable through hiring and training. Her belief that outbound was unscalable reflected a skill deficiency in building sales teams, not a physical constraint on the model.

Alex Hormozi conducted approximately 4,000 one-on-one sales closes (not consultations, but full closes) over a multi-year period at his gym locations. He scheduled two to three prospects every 30 minutes back-to-back, pitching the same offer repeatedly. No formal sales training program was attended; the volume of real closes was the training. By the end, people would ask Hormozi which sales training program he had completed, and his answer was that the unscalable repetition itself was the training.

Gary Halbert, the direct-mail copywriter, used an extreme hypothetical to force maximum creative effort when writing a sales letter: he imagined he could only write one letter in his lifetime or he would die. Starting from that constraint, he would specify a handwritten envelope with the recipient's name handwritten, a lick-and-stamp, a handwritten personal letter inside, and a lumpy physical insert. He began with the impossible extreme to identify every high-impact element, then looked for which elements could be scaled once the letter's performance was proven.

Alex Hormozi described a company in their portfolio that still does group onboarding at the time the video was recorded and has scaled to over $100 million per year in revenue. The company recognized that onboarding was a critical inflection point for setting expectations and making and keeping promises, so it invested in systematizing group onboarding rather than eliminating it. One person can run six sessions of 30 per day, reaching 180 customers per day, and a trained second person doubles that with no degradation in process quality.

Alex Hormozi gave a weight-loss analogy to explain premature concern about scale: a prospective gym member saying they do not want to get too bulky before they have even started working out. The person has no muscle yet but is worried about a problem that is years of training away. In business, the equivalent is a founder with $0 in revenue refusing to take sales calls because the tactic is unscalable at $100M. The problem the founder is worrying about does not exist at their current stage.

Alex Hormozi described the sales process for a $20/month community membership as an example of a seemingly low-ticket product that still benefits from founder-led phone sales. He compared it to gym memberships, which are sold by a dedicated salesperson at the front desk, not the gym owner, proving that even low-price recurring memberships can be scaled through a sales role without founder involvement.

Alex Hormozi described a fintech founder who had recently exited for $2.5 billion. In a phone conversation that week, the fintech founder told Hormozi that the entire key to his success was the unscalable work: the one-on-one calls, the deep customer conversations in the early stages that most business owners refuse to do because they label them unscalable. The fintech founder and Hormozi both found it ironic that the path to a $2.5B exit ran directly through high-touch, low-tech customer engagement.

Alex Hormozi described an agency owner as a concrete done-for-you example. An agency taking on full-service clients must build SOPs for lead magnets, ads, landing pages, upsell pages, and email follow-up. Once those SOPs exist, the agency can launch a done-with-you tier where clients follow the same systems with guidance rather than full service, and then a do-it-yourself tier where clients receive the SOPs directly. Each tier is productized from the done-for-you work done at the prior stage.

practices.text: Get on the phone with every customer regardless of ticket price when you have available time and low revenue; the learning from each call compounds into better marketing, better product, and higher conversion.
Start any new product line or business at the done-for-you tier first, develop the SOPs from live client work, then systematically introduce done-with-you and do-it-yourself tiers downstream.
When evaluating a tactic as unscalable, reframe the question: if you had unlimited money and unlimited talent, could you scale it? If yes, the constraint is resources and skill, not physics.
Ask every batch of new customers the two magic questions (irreplaceable feature and removable feature) repeatedly to maintain a current power ranking of product value across your customer base.

Use the Gary Halbert maximum-constraint thought experiment when designing any high-touch outreach: design it as if this single piece will determine your survival, then strip it back only after you know which elements drive the result.

When your sales reps use a chat interface or automation, switch to personal iPhones with personalized voice notes or video messages; the personalization signal lifts response rates and is scalable by buying phones for the team.
Onboard every new customer personally even at $10/month; customers who are personally onboarded stay longer, refer more, and provide better product feedback.
